A: Maya's software company offered her the lead architect role, but it requires relocating to Toronto for eighteen months. Taking it would put her on track for an executive position, while leaving means missing Sunday dinners and the daily support she shares with her recently widowed sister. Should Maya accept the promotion or remain near her family?
B: After years painting sets for the same neighborhood theater, Luis has been invited to design a major touring production. The contract could establish his national reputation, yet rehearsals would keep him away through the final season with the close ensemble that trained him and depends on his presence. Should Luis join the tour or finish the season with his theater community?
C: A payment outage has trapped thousands of customers at checkout, and Priya is the only engineer who understands the failing service. She has a severe migraine and her doctor told her to rest in darkness, but the overnight support team cannot restore purchases without her guidance. Should Priya log in to lead the repair or protect her health and sleep?

A: Nora has been offered a solo exhibition at a prestigious Berlin gallery during the month her local printmaking collective is preparing its tenth anniversary show. Berlin could transform her career, but accepting would leave the five artists who built the collective with her to mount their milestone event alone. Should Nora pursue the solo exhibition or stay with her longtime collaborators?
B: A professional cycling team wants Darius to attend its distant development camp immediately, giving him his first credible route into elite racing. His neighborhood club, where his closest friends train together, is entering a regional relay that same month and has no replacement rider. Should Darius leave for the development camp or race beside his club?
C: Elena bought a demanding piano method course to prepare for an audition six months away. Tonight's scheduled practice covers scales she dislikes, while her favorite film has just appeared online and her friends are gathering to watch it with takeout. Skipping one evening would feel pleasant but weaken the routine she needs to improve. Should Elena practice or join the film night?

A: Jonah can enter an accelerated doctoral program that promises early publications and a strong academic career, but its schedule would end the weekly study circle he has shared with three close classmates since freshman year. Staying in the regular program preserves those friendships and their mutual support but slows his progress. Should Jonah accelerate alone or continue alongside his study group?
B: The owner of a renowned vineyard has offered Amara an apprenticeship that could lead to managing her own estate. It begins during harvest, when her family's small farm relies on everyone working and eating together, a tradition that has kept the household close for decades. Should Amara take the vineyard opportunity or spend another harvest with her family?
C: A school board wants new history workbooks distributed before Monday so classes can start the revised curriculum on time. Editor Caleb found conflicting dates and poorly sourced maps that require another week to verify; delaying leaves teachers without materials, while printing now may put lasting errors in every classroom. Should Caleb approve immediate printing or hold the workbooks for careful correction?

A: Ravi has qualified for a national young farmers competition whose winner receives enough investment to expand a greenhouse business. The final occurs during the cooperative's annual planting weekend, when his closest neighbors share equipment and count on his seed drill. Should Ravi travel to compete for expansion funding or plant beside the cooperative that has supported him?
B: Promotion to district fire captain would give Tessa greater responsibility and the career she has worked toward, but the post uses rotating stations across the county. She would lose daily shifts with the crew whose members helped raise her children and gather at her home every Friday. Should Tessa accept the captaincy or remain with her current station crew?
C: After twisting his knee, orchard manager Owen was told to avoid slopes for a week. A sudden frost is forecast tonight, and two inexperienced workers need him to guide the placement of heaters among the hillside trees; without him, much of the crop may be lost. Should Owen work the orchard despite the risk of worsening his injury or follow his recovery instructions?

A: Selene's bakery has been selected for a lucrative airport concession that could turn her single shop into a regional brand. Running it requires closing the original counter for six months, ending the morning routine she shares with loyal staff and neighbors who helped the bakery survive. Should Selene pursue the airport expansion or keep serving her established neighborhood circle?
B: Kenji's friends built a small open-source project together after work, and their weekly sessions became his main social anchor. A venture fund now wants him to develop it full-time in San Francisco without the others, offering the chance to create a major company. Should Kenji relocate to pursue the venture or keep building with his close-knit team?
C: For forty years, Ana's family restaurant has handwritten every order and displayed the paper tickets along the kitchen rail. A tablet system would reduce mistakes and simplify accounting, but her parents and regular customers see the visible tickets as part of the restaurant's character. Should Ana introduce digital ordering or preserve the family's familiar method?

A: Biologist Evan has saved a small emergency fund while working on short contracts. His former lab technician calls because her elderly cat needs surgery by Friday and she cannot cover the final eight hundred dollars; lending it may save the cat but leave Evan unable to pay rent if his contract ends. Should Evan provide the surgery money or preserve his emergency savings?
B: Adjunct lecturer Farah has enough set aside to replace her unreliable car before winter. A student she mentors has been accepted to a teaching conference but cannot afford the registration and train fare, and missing it could close an early career opportunity. Should Farah fund the student's trip or keep the money for dependable transportation?
C: During a joint experiment, Leah discovers that her longtime colleague Marcus entered several measurements incorrectly, making their celebrated result unsupported. Reporting the error before publication protects the scientific record but could cost Marcus his fellowship and damage a friendship built over twelve years. Should Leah disclose the faulty measurements to the journal or protect Marcus from the consequences?

A: Semi-professional goalkeeper Malik has saved his match fees for physiotherapy after recurring shoulder pain. His teammate's guide dog develops an infection requiring immediate treatment, and the teammate cannot cover the clinic deposit until payday. Paying would help the dog today but could leave Malik unable to treat his own injury. Should Malik cover the veterinary deposit or retain his therapy savings?
B: Library assistant Grace keeps three months of rent untouched because her hours may soon be cut. A coworker whose apartment flooded needs a hotel room for herself and her young son tonight, and local shelters are full. Should Grace pay for their temporary room or keep the money that protects her own housing if her income falls?
C: A rowing club asks captain Imani to tell the full team about her panic attacks after one struck during practice. Sharing the details could help teammates respond calmly and explain her occasional absences, but it would expose medical information she has kept private even from friends. Should Imani discuss her panic attacks with the team or keep that part of her life confidential?

A: Nurse Daniel keeps cash for a deposit on a safer apartment after repeated break-ins on his street. A discharged patient he has come to know needs a portable oxygen battery that insurance will not cover, and without it she cannot attend her daughter's wedding. Should Daniel buy the battery for her or protect his plan to move?
B: Mei reserved the month's remaining shop income to repair the freezer that protects her catering inventory. Her longtime delivery driver faces eviction with his daughter after an unexpected medical bill and asks for the exact amount Mei saved. Should Mei lend him the money and risk spoiled stock or secure the equipment her business depends on?
C: A rural hospital offers resident physician Sofia a competitive surgical fellowship that would speed her path toward becoming a specialist. Accepting means leaving the small ward team and patients she has served for three years, including colleagues who became her closest friends. Should Sofia take the fellowship or remain with the hospital community where she belongs?

A: Bus dispatcher Andre has saved enough to cover his mortgage during the agency's expected summer layoffs. A driver on his shift needs a specialized hearing aid to remain licensed, but her insurer denied the claim and she may lose her job next week. Should Andre help purchase the hearing aid or preserve his mortgage reserve?
B: Chemist Rosa planned to use her modest patent payment to clear a high-interest credit card. A graduate assistant in her lab needs dental surgery for a painful infection and has no family who can help, but covering it would keep Rosa in debt for another year. Should Rosa pay for the assistant's surgery or restore her own financial stability?
C: City planner Theo wants to replace two downtown parking lanes with protected bicycle lanes after studying the crash data. His parents, neighbors, and longtime friends all oppose the change and expect him to defend local parking at the public hearing. Should Theo present his preferred bicycle plan or endorse the position that would retain their approval?

A: Nadia has put aside the stipend from organizing a community garden to replace her broken laptop, which she needs for paid freelance work. A volunteer she knows is sleeping in his car and needs the same amount for a room deposit before cold weather arrives. Should Nadia fund his deposit or keep the money for her essential work equipment?
B: Ceramicist Joel keeps his market earnings as a cushion for months when few pieces sell. A fellow studio member's kiln accident injured her rabbit, and the emergency clinic requires payment tonight that she cannot raise. Should Joel use his cushion to cover the rabbit's treatment or retain the savings that steady his own uncertain income?
C: While coordinating a neighborhood playground rebuild, Aisha learns that she previously received treatment for a gambling addiction. Telling the volunteer committee could explain why she insists on dual signatures for every purchase and encourage frank financial oversight, but it would reveal a history she has shared with almost nobody. Should Aisha disclose her past to the committee or keep it private?

A: Devon promised to supervise a critical database migration because the junior engineers have never performed one. On the scheduled night, he develops a high fever and dizziness; postponement would interrupt a client's launch, but staying online until dawn may deepen his illness. Should Devon lead the migration as promised or stop working to recover?
B: Midwife Hana has completed a double shift when a patient she supported throughout pregnancy goes into complicated labor. The replacement midwife is qualified but unfamiliar with the patient's history, while Hana is shaking from fatigue and needs sleep to recover safely. Should Hana remain for the birth she promised to attend or hand over care and rest?
C: Developer Arjun can spend a month experimenting with an unfamiliar database that might make his new app remarkably flexible, though its limitations are still unclear. The proven system offers predictable performance and reliable backups but restricts several features he hopes to discover. Should Arjun explore the uncertain technology or build with the safer established platform?

A: Stage manager Ruth promised to call every cue for her community theater's opening night, and no understudy knows the complicated lighting sequence. Hours before curtain she experiences chest pain and is advised to seek immediate evaluation; canceling disappoints a sold-out audience, while continuing could endanger her health. Should Ruth go to the hospital or fulfill her opening-night responsibility?
B: Cafe owner Ben has bronchitis and his doctor prescribed two days of complete rest. His only employee calls out just before a prepaid memorial reception, leaving the grieving family without the meal Ben agreed to provide. Should Ben open the kitchen and honor the booking or close the cafe to protect his recovery?
C: A gallery charges every exhibitor the same late fee when work arrives after the installation deadline. Curator Mina's former teacher misses it because she has been caring for her terminally ill husband and cannot afford the charge, though others have paid after difficult weeks. Should Mina waive the fee for her teacher or enforce the rule equally?

A: Teacher Malcolm promised his graduating class a final weekend review before their licensing exam. On Saturday morning he wakes with laryngitis and a fever; the substitute does not know the material, yet speaking for four hours could prolong his illness. Should Malcolm conduct the review his students rely on or cancel it and recover?
B: Janelle coordinates volunteers rebuilding a wheelchair ramp for an elderly neighbor, and the concrete delivery cannot be moved. A strained back makes lifting painful, while several first-time volunteers need her hands-on direction to finish before rain arrives. Should Janelle work through the pain to meet her commitment or stay home and let her back heal?
C: Professor Wei is invited to deliver a short keynote overseas, an appearance likely to raise his profile and consulting income. The trip requires two long flights for a twenty-minute talk, despite an equally useful video option, adding emissions that contribute to a burden shared far beyond the conference. Should Wei fly for the career benefit or present remotely to limit that impact?

A: Dairy farmer Elise promised her brother she would cover the predawn milking while he attended his daughter's graduation. She develops food poisoning overnight, and no relief worker is available; leaving the herd waiting creates distress and lost production, but entering the barn while weak may worsen her condition. Should Elise complete the milking or remain in bed to recover?
B: Cellist Anton's quartet is recording the final movement today after months of shared preparation. His wrist has become swollen and numb, and the specialist warned that continued playing could turn a minor injury into lasting damage, but canceling forfeits the rented studio and everyone's work. Should Anton perform his part or withdraw to protect his hand?
C: Every winter, Lila prunes her apple trees before buds emerge, producing healthier branches and a stronger autumn crop. This mild afternoon is her last available chance, but the work is repetitive and she would rather sit by the fire with a new novel and cider. Should Lila complete the pruning or enjoy the comfortable afternoon indoors?

A: Tailor Simone has promised forty altered uniforms to a restaurant opening tomorrow. A sudden eye infection makes close stitching painful and her doctor advised avoiding detailed work, but the restaurant cannot postpone its opening and her assistant cannot finish alone. Should Simone sew through the evening to deliver the uniforms or stop and protect her eyesight?
B: Goalkeeper Pavel agreed to play in the amateur league final because his club has no reserve. After a fall at work, he has a suspected concussion and needs monitoring, yet withdrawing would force ten teammates to forfeit the match they trained all year to reach. Should Pavel honor his commitment to play or sit out for his health?
C: Bookshop owner Clara charges every vendor the same nonrefundable fee for canceling an event within forty-eight hours. A debut author cancels because her child has been hospitalized and asks Clara to return money needed for travel, although two other vendors recently paid the fee. Should Clara grant this hardship exception or apply the cancellation policy equally?

A: Marine researcher Soraya can join an exploratory voyage to an unmapped vent field where the crew may discover unknown species, but weather and sampling success are uncertain. A funded laboratory placement offers guaranteed data, a fixed schedule, and established methods, though little room for discovery. Should Soraya take the open-ended voyage or choose the predictable laboratory project?
B: Residents give Mateo a vacant lot for a summer community project. He can let volunteers improvise gardens, play areas, and gathering spaces as ideas emerge, risking unfinished work, or follow a contractor's fixed plan for a modest park with certified equipment and a guaranteed opening date. Should Mateo support the evolving volunteer design or select the dependable standard plan?
C: At her institute's annual field survey, geologist Nia wants to replace handwritten notebooks with tablets that attach coordinates and photographs to each observation. The senior team values the marked paper volumes used for fifty years and fears losing the craft of careful field notes. Should Nia introduce digital records or continue the institute's longstanding notebook tradition?

A: Climber Felix has one free day in the Dolomites and can attempt an unmarked ridge that promises new views but has uncertain rock conditions. The local guide recommends a protected route with reliable anchors and an exact descent time, though Felix has climbed it twice before. Should Felix explore the unknown ridge or take the secure familiar route?
B: Programmer Yasmin is choosing the foundation for a personal game. An experimental engine would let her invent unusual physics and perhaps produce something distinctive, but documentation is incomplete and the project may fail; a mature engine supplies tested tools and predictable results within her vacation. Should Yasmin explore the experimental engine or use the reliable established one?
C: A youth football league needs replacement goalposts before Saturday's tournament. Fabricator Hugo can weld a basic set by Friday, allowing every match to proceed, or spend another week reinforcing joints and applying weatherproof coating for a safer, longer-lasting finish. Should Hugo deliver the workable goalposts in time or delay the tournament to complete them properly?

A: After standard therapies fail, patient coordinator Lena can enroll Mr. Harris in a new trial whose benefits and side effects remain uncertain. A conventional treatment is unlikely to cure him but has a well-known course and can reliably control symptoms for months. Should Lena encourage the experimental possibility or recommend the predictable treatment plan?
B: Runner Keisha has qualified for a trail race where competitors choose their own route between mountain checkpoints, offering adventure but uncertain terrain and finish times. A road race that weekend follows closed streets, staffed aid stations, and a pace she can forecast. Should Keisha enter the open-route trail event or choose the controlled road race?
C: Pharmacist Omar notices that his longtime friend, a physician, prescribed twice the recommended dose to a child. Alerting the hospital would correct the record and protect the patient, but an investigation could end his friend's struggling practice after one mistake. Should Omar report the dosing error or shield his friend from professional harm?

A: Transit planner Evelyn can test an on-demand night bus whose route changes with passenger requests, potentially reaching isolated residents but producing uncertain wait times. Keeping the fixed loop guarantees published stops and dependable timing, although several neighborhoods remain beyond walking distance. Should Evelyn pilot the flexible service or retain the predictable fixed route?
B: For his final university term, Lucas can design an independent course around archival material nobody has catalogued, with no assurance the work will yield a coherent thesis. A standard seminar provides a proven syllabus, frequent grading, and a clear path to graduation. Should Lucas pursue the uncertain independent study or enroll in the structured seminar?
C: The town clerk wants residents to book appointments through a new online portal that could shorten queues and send automatic reminders. Older staff and many longtime residents value the walk-in counter and the numbered paper tickets used since the municipal hall opened. Should the clerk adopt online booking or preserve the familiar public-service routine?

A: A neighborhood association gives Inez funds for a riverfront mural but no final design. She can invite residents to paint whatever develops over the weekend, risking a disjointed result, or hire a studio offering an approved sketch, insured painters, and guaranteed completion. Should Inez open the wall to uncertain collaboration or commission the predictable professional design?
B: Park ranger Cole can lead visitors into a newly opened wetland where wildlife sightings and trail conditions are unpredictable. The established boardwalk tour has railings, mapped stops, and a reliable return time but reveals little beyond familiar habitats. Should Cole offer the exploratory wetland walk or keep the group on the protected boardwalk route?
C: Organizer Fatima has been invited to direct a national housing coalition, a position that could give her campaigns far greater influence. Accepting requires leaving the tenant group whose members meet in her kitchen and have shared years of victories and setbacks. Should Fatima pursue the national leadership role or remain with her close neighborhood organization?

A: Engineer Becca learns that her close friend quietly copied licensed code into the startup's new product and told managers it was original. Revealing the source prevents a false release and possible legal trouble, but her friend would likely be fired days before his wedding. Should Becca tell the managers what she found or protect her friend by staying silent?
B: Physicist Samuel reviews a paper written by his former supervisor and discovers that its strongest graph omits several measurements that contradict the conclusion. Correcting the record may trigger a retraction and damage the mentor who launched his career, while silence lets a misleading result stand. Should Samuel report the missing measurements or remain loyal to his mentor?
C: App designer Lotte prefers a quiet interface with no engagement streaks, believing users should decide when to return. Her investors and colleagues insist on daily badges and warn that rejecting them will make her seem difficult before promotion decisions. Should Lotte build the restrained product she believes in or add the features that would win the team's approval?

A: Museum registrar Celia discovers that a painting donated by her uncle has documentation proving it was taken from a family during wartime. Disclosing the records could force restitution and publicly disgrace the relative who financed her education, while concealing them preserves a false ownership history. Should Celia reveal the painting's provenance or protect her uncle's reputation?
B: Ecologist Bram realizes that his research partner and closest friend counted the same bird colony twice in a report already sent to conservation officials. Correcting the figure could cost her a grant and embarrass their lab, but leaving it unchallenged misstates the population. Should Bram notify the officials of the error or stand by his friend?
C: Choreographer Nadine has built a new dance around movements she developed during treatment for depression. Explaining that history to the company could help dancers understand the piece and invite more honest collaboration, but it would expose deeply personal medical details. Should Nadine share the origin of the dance or keep her experience private?

A: School counselor Irene learns that her colleague and friend altered a senior's attendance record so the student could graduate. Reporting the change restores an accurate transcript but may cost the colleague her job and strain a decade-long friendship; silence protects her while preserving false information. Should Irene inform the principal or remain loyal to her friend?
B: Surgeon Malik notices that his longtime operating partner documented a procedure as complication-free despite a sponge being briefly left inside the patient and removed. Correcting the chart may bring disciplinary action against someone he trusts, yet the current record hides clinically relevant truth. Should Malik amend the chart and report the incident or protect his partner?
C: Tutor Grace promised to supervise six anxious students through an overnight mathematics competition. She develops a severe asthma flare shortly before departure, and no other teacher knows the travel arrangements; canceling would end their participation, but attending means hours away from her usual clinic. Should Grace accompany the students as promised or withdraw to protect her breathing?

A: Farm inspector Alice finds that her cousin has been labeling ordinary eggs as free-range after storm damage confined the hens indoors. Recording the violation protects accurate sales information but could cancel the contract keeping his farm afloat, while overlooking it shields a relative through a difficult season. Should Alice file the truthful report or protect her cousin's livelihood?
B: Nurse Theo learns that his closest coworker changed a patient's fall time in the chart to make it appear that staffing rules were followed. Correcting the entry preserves an honest medical record but could lead to her suspension and leave her family without wages. Should Theo report the altered time or remain loyal to his coworker?
C: Young farmer Mira wants to replace part of the family wheat field with the herbs she enjoys growing and has already found local buyers. Her parents and neighboring farmers expect her to continue the crop that defines the family farm and dismiss herbs as unserious. Should Mira plant according to her own preference or keep wheat to retain their approval?

A: While preparing quarterly accounts, florist Dana discovers that her brother and co-owner has been deleting cash sales from the tax records. Correcting the return would expose his actions, bring penalties, and possibly break their partnership, but signing the current figures makes her endorse a lie. Should Dana report the true sales or protect her brother and their shop?
B: Jon reviews receipts for a neighborhood food pantry and sees that his closest friend claimed reimbursement for supplies she never purchased. Revealing the false claim would preserve an honest grant report but could remove her from the committee and end their friendship during a difficult divorce. Should Jon correct the accounts publicly or remain loyal to his friend?
C: A beverage distributor offers cafe owner Suki a profitable contract if she switches from washable glasses to individually wrapped plastic cups. The savings would fund a second location and raise her income, while thousands of discarded cups would add waste collected and processed by the whole city. Should Suki accept the contract for expansion or keep reusable service to reduce the wider burden?

A: Astronomer Peter needs to classify telescope images for ninety minutes each evening if he wants a complete dataset by spring. Tonight the work is monotonous, his apartment is warm, and a new detective series is ready to stream. Missing the session brings immediate relaxation but weakens the routine behind months of progress. Should Peter analyze the images or settle onto the sofa?
B: Swimmer Amina plans six months of early pool sessions to improve her turns before regional trials. Rain drums against the window at 5 a.m., and staying under the blankets would be far more pleasant than crossing town for repetitive drills, though another missed practice slows the improvement she wants. Should Amina get up and train or enjoy another two hours in bed?
C: A laboratory requires every researcher who misses equipment training to wait a month for the next session. Manager Colin learns that a new assistant was absent because she was caring for her injured father and will lose her summer placement if she waits, while others followed the rule. Should Colin arrange an exception for her or enforce the same schedule for everyone?

A: Basketball referee Leon wants to qualify for the national league and must review one recorded match every night to sharpen his calls. His friends have reserved a table at his favorite pub after a tiring day, while the video session offers only slow, solitary work toward a distant goal. Should Leon study the match or spend the evening relaxing with friends?
B: Beekeeper Salma must inspect and record one hive each afternoon to learn which colonies need stronger queens next season. Today the air is hot, the protective suit is uncomfortable, and a shaded hammock offers an easy nap, but delaying will leave gaps in the breeding records. Should Salma complete the inspection or rest in the shade?
C: Tennis coach Robin saved tournament earnings to replace a cracked roof before the rainy season. A junior player she knows cannot afford a wheelchair designed for competitive tennis and may leave the club without it; buying the chair would keep him playing but put Robin's home repair at risk. Should Robin purchase the wheelchair or retain her roofing fund?

A: Medical student Isaac has committed to practicing surgical knots for forty minutes after each shift so his hands are ready for clinical assessment. Tonight he can continue the tedious drills in an empty classroom or join his housemates for pizza and board games downstairs. Should Isaac maintain the practice routine or take the easy, enjoyable evening with his housemates?
B: Postal worker Marie is studying street maps each night to qualify for a better route assignment in three months. After dinner, memorizing unfamiliar addresses feels dull beside a soft chair and a half-finished mystery novel, but repeated study is the only way she will pass. Should Marie open the maps and study or spend the evening reading for pleasure?
C: Clinic administrator Faisal learns that his trusted deputy changed the time on a medication log to hide a late dose. Reporting the accurate time may lead to her dismissal after fifteen years together, while accepting the altered entry leaves the patient's record false and blocks a proper review. Should Faisal restore and report the true time or protect his loyal deputy?

A: Archivist Paula intends to index twenty municipal photographs each Saturday until the neglected collection becomes searchable. A sunny morning invites her to linger over coffee on the balcony, and nobody expects immediate results, yet postponing the repetitive entries will keep residents waiting months longer. Should Paula complete today's indexing target or enjoy an unstructured morning off?
B: Ramon is teaching himself programming by solving one difficult exercise before playing games each evening. Today's problem has resisted him for an hour, while his friends are already online starting a tournament; leaving it preserves a fun night but interrupts the steady effort needed to change careers. Should Ramon keep working through the exercise or join the game now?
C: The water department can reopen a repaired neighborhood pipe by noon if supervisor Beth approves the standard pressure test. She wants an additional camera inspection to catch hidden cracks, which would improve reliability but leave homes without water until evening. Should Beth restore service quickly after the basic test or delay it for the more thorough inspection?

A: Every Wednesday, Omar spends two hours updating donor records for a volunteer-run youth center so its next funding application will be accurate. Tonight the entries are especially repetitive, and neighbors are holding a barbecue in the courtyard, but skipping them will create a larger backlog. Should Omar finish the records as planned or go downstairs to enjoy the barbecue?
B: Graduate researcher Chloe must calibrate a sensor at dawn each day for six weeks to produce comparable readings. Tomorrow's forecast is cold and gray, and she could stay in her warm room after a late film, though one missing measurement would weaken the series. Should Chloe rise for the calibration or sleep through the uncomfortable morning?
C: Treasurer Emmett has reserved the neighborhood cleanup fund for protective gloves and waste bins needed next month. A volunteer's elderly dog needs urgent dental treatment, and she asks to borrow the fund until her next paycheck; helping could relieve the animal's pain but leave the cleanup unequipped. Should Emmett lend her the money or safeguard the project's limited resources?

A: Junior developer Iris wants to specialize in accessibility engineering because she finds the work meaningful. Her parents and senior teammates urge her toward cybersecurity, a prestigious specialty they understand, and warn that choosing otherwise will disappoint mentors supporting her promotion. Should Iris follow her own technical interest or choose cybersecurity to retain their approval?
B: Noah wants to study culinary history for his university elective, although his family considers it frivolous and expects another economics course. His friends also plan to take economics together and say he will isolate himself by leaving. Should Noah enroll in the subject that interests him or choose economics to satisfy the people close to him?
C: For two decades, a software cooperative has opened every release meeting by reading customer letters aloud. New director Vera proposes an online dashboard that groups feedback instantly and frees an hour for engineering, but veteran members regard the readings as a ritual connecting them to users. Should Vera adopt the dashboard or preserve the cooperative's established meeting custom?

A: Illustrator Benicio wants his next exhibit to feature stark charcoal portraits, although his gallery owner and relatives prefer the bright landscapes that made him popular. They say the darker work will embarrass supporters attending the opening and may stop recommending him. Should Benicio show the portraits he wants to make or paint landscapes that preserve their approval?
B: Librarian Heather prefers to move the children's reading hour outdoors, where stories could include walks and noisy games. Her colleagues and parent committee expect the quiet indoor format and suggest she is being unprofessional by changing it. Should Heather run the lively outdoor program she favors or keep the familiar format to satisfy them?
C: Dancer Kwame receives an offer to join a celebrated contemporary company that could make him an international soloist. Its two-year tour would remove him from the small cultural center where he rehearses daily with childhood friends and teaches their children. Should Kwame accept the career-making tour or remain rooted in the artistic community that raised him?

A: Graduate student Leila wants to write her thesis on informal learning in repair cafes, a subject her committee considers marginal. Her parents and classmates praise a conventional topic on corporate training and expect her to choose the respectable path. Should Leila research the question that fascinates her or select the approved topic to keep their confidence?
B: Barber Dominic wants to close his shop on Mondays and use the day for woodworking, even though his family and neighboring merchants say a serious owner should remain open six days. They warn that customers will judge his commitment. Should Dominic set the schedule that suits his life or keep Monday hours to maintain their respect?
C: Teacher Ava can take students into the city without a fixed itinerary, letting unexpected exhibits and conversations shape their history project, though the day may yield little usable work. A guided museum package guarantees supervised transport, scheduled lessons, and assessed worksheets. Should Ava choose the open-ended city exploration or book the predictable educational program?

A: Shepherd Erin prefers breeding a hardy local sheep that thrives on her rocky land, while her family and farming association favor a fashionable commercial breed. They imply that continuing with local animals proves she lacks ambition and may exclude her from their breeding group. Should Erin follow her own judgment or adopt the breed that wins their approval?
B: Research assistant Victor wants to leave a prominent genetics lab for a smaller ecology project that better fits his curiosity. His professors and parents celebrate the famous lab and say departing would waste their recommendations and reflect poorly on him. Should Victor choose the research he prefers or remain where respected people expect him to work?
C: After pesticide exposure, vineyard owner Celeste begins counseling for anxiety and insomnia. Telling her seasonal workers could explain new safety procedures and encourage them to report symptoms openly, but it would reveal mental health details she has kept within her family. Should Celeste disclose her treatment to the crew or keep her medical experience private?

A: Greengrocer Hassan wants to stop stocking imported luxury fruit and focus on affordable seasonal produce. His business partners and adult children say the change looks unsophisticated and expect him to maintain the upscale image they proudly promote. Should Hassan shape the shop around his own priorities or keep the luxury range to preserve their approval?
B: Composer Yara wants to score a playful children's puppet show, but her conservatory peers and conductor parents expect another serious chamber work. They suggest the puppet project will make them ashamed to introduce her as a composer. Should Yara accept the work that delights her or write the formal piece that would earn their respect?
C: Repair shop owner Tomas is offered a national franchise license that could triple revenue and make him a prominent entrepreneur. Expansion would require leaving the workshop where his cousins, neighbors, and oldest friends work beside him each day. Should Tomas pursue the franchise opportunity or remain with the close local team that built the shop together?

A: A botanical institute has pressed every new specimen into handmade paper folders since its founding. Curator Aditi can introduce sealed digital imaging stations that preserve fragile colors and allow remote study, but older botanists fear abandoning the tactile catalog that links generations of researchers. Should Aditi modernize specimen recording or continue the institute's traditional method?
B: At Raul's neighborhood shoe shop, customers have always watched repairs at a front workbench and talked with the cobbler. Moving production behind a wall would allow modern machinery and faster service, but longtime patrons treasure the visible craft as part of every visit. Should Raul redesign the shop around the new equipment or preserve its open workbench tradition?
C: A private company offers oceanographer Mae a generous fee to conduct coral surveys by helicopter, allowing her to finish quickly and accept more contracts. Boats would take longer and pay her less, but repeated flights consume far more fuel and add emissions whose effects fall broadly on coastal ecosystems and communities. Should Mae choose the lucrative helicopter surveys or use the slower, lower-impact boats?

A: For seventy years, Harbor Rowing Club has selected crews through timed trials on the same stretch of river. Coach Mila wants to use indoor power data and video analysis instead, giving athletes more precise feedback, but alumni see the river trial as the ceremony that binds each generation. Should Mila adopt data-based selection or preserve the traditional river trials?
B: Residents have always begun their spring cleanup by gathering at dawn and drawing street assignments from an old wooden box. Coordinator Theo could replace the ritual with an app that assigns routes efficiently and tracks missed areas, but neighbors treasure the shared opening. Should Theo introduce the app or keep the familiar draw that marks the season?
C: Cricket umpire Sanjay promised to officiate a youth semifinal after another official withdrew. On match morning, severe back spasms make standing painful, and canceling would leave both teams unable to play, but six hours on the field could worsen his injury. Should Sanjay fulfill the officiating duty or withdraw to protect his recovery?

A: The maternity ward has recorded every newborn's footprint on a paper card kept by the family since the hospital opened. Director June proposes secure digital scans that are clearer and easier to retrieve, but nurses and parents value the inked card as a tangible rite. Should June replace the cards with digital records or preserve the footprint tradition?
B: A village orchestra has tuned to the same local pitch and opened concerts with its founder's march for generations. New conductor Pavel wants standard tuning and rotating contemporary openings so visiting musicians can join easily, while members fear losing their distinctive sound and ritual. Should Pavel modernize the orchestra's practice or continue its inherited musical customs?
C: A clinic removes patients from its waiting list after two missed appointments. Receptionist Alma learns that a homeless patient missed both because his shelter repeatedly changed locations; restoring him helps someone in hardship but bypasses others who complied and kept waiting. Should Alma make an exception for him or apply the same removal rule to every patient?

A: For decades, the courthouse has announced each morning's cases from a clerk's handwritten board in the entrance hall. Administrator Rosa wants electronic displays with live updates and translations, but veteran clerks and attorneys consider the board part of the building's civic character. Should Rosa install the displays or continue the courthouse's handwritten announcement tradition?
B: At a century-old baseball ground, attendants still change inning numbers by hand on a wooden scoreboard. The club can install a bright digital screen with instant statistics, but supporters value watching the attendant work and regard the board as part of every game. Should the club modernize the scoreboard or preserve the manual ritual?
C: A sanitation contractor offers inspector Greg free household trash collection if he approves diesel trucks that barely meet current limits. The perk would save him substantial fees, while the trucks would add noise and exhaust along routes serving thousands of residents. Should Greg accept the private benefit and approve the fleet or reject it to limit the community-wide cost?

A: Neighbors building the annual lantern festival have always shaped bamboo frames together in the school gym. Organizer Mei could order reusable metal frames that assemble faster and survive rain, but older volunteers say hand-building lanterns is where newcomers learn the community's stories. Should Mei switch to metal frames or retain the shared bamboo-making tradition?
B: The Bell family has harvested olives by spreading cloths and combing branches by hand for four generations. Daughter Lucia proposes a mechanical shaker that would finish before autumn storms and reduce labor, but her grandparents regard the communal hand harvest as the farm's defining custom. Should Lucia introduce the machine or continue harvesting in the traditional way?
C: Community garden chair Ezra discovers that his longtime friend submitted photographs from last year to claim completion of a current grant milestone. Reporting the truth could revoke funding and force his friend off the committee, while accepting the images misleads the foundation. Should Ezra correct the grant report or protect the friend who helped establish the garden?

A: A coding bootcamp gives every applicant exactly seventy-two hours to complete its entry project. Reviewer Nikhil learns that one applicant lost electricity throughout the deadline after her building burned, and she asks for three extra days, although previous late submissions were rejected. Should Nikhil grant her an extension or enforce the same deadline for everyone?
B: Volunteers receive one garden plot only if they attend three winter planning meetings. Coordinator Val knows a single father missed them while caring for a hospitalized child and needs the plot to grow food, but others arranged difficult schedules to qualify. Should Val waive the attendance rule for him or allocate plots strictly by the published requirement?
C: A hospital needs a medication-tracking update deployed by Friday before a regulatory inspection. Developer Ari can release the working version after limited testing, or spend another week checking rare dosage combinations and improving error messages, leaving staff on the old system during inspection. Should Ari deliver the update quickly or delay it to ensure dependable quality?

A: A dance academy bars students from the annual performance after more than four absences. Director Opal knows one talented dancer missed five rehearsals while moving between foster homes and sees how much the performance matters to her, while other students met the requirement. Should Opal let the dancer perform or apply the attendance rule equally?
B: A software conference refunds no tickets within seven days of opening. Organizer Dae receives a request from a freelancer whose premature baby requires unexpected hospital care; the ticket cost would help him travel to the child, although other late cancellations received nothing. Should Dae issue a compassionate refund or uphold the same policy for all attendees?
C: Sculptor Ines saved her commission payment to replace unsafe wiring in her studio before winter. A neighboring artist's dog is struck by a car and needs surgery tonight, but using the savings would leave Ines working around a serious electrical risk. Should Ines pay for the dog's treatment or keep the money for her own safety?

A: Professor Ahmed deducts ten points from every essay submitted after noon. One student delivers hers that evening after spending the morning translating for her mother at an asylum hearing, and the penalty would make her fail, while classmates accepted deductions for other emergencies. Should Ahmed excuse this late essay or apply the announced penalty equally?
B: A junior football academy releases any player who misses three mandatory practices. Coach Bruna's fastest winger reaches that limit because his family was evicted and he spent nights changing shelters, but several substitutes maintained perfect attendance. Should Bruna keep him on the squad because of his hardship or enforce the rule applied to everyone else?
C: Student adviser Milo wants to create a quiet woodworking club, although his parents and faculty colleagues consider it unsuitable for someone pursuing school leadership. They expect him to run the prestigious debate society and say senior staff will respect that choice. Should Milo start the club he personally wants or lead debate to gain their approval?

A: A farming cooperative fines members who deliver grain above the agreed moisture limit. Treasurer Ruth receives a damp load from an elderly farmer whose dryer failed and whose medical bills consumed his repair money; waiving the fine helps him survive but treats compliant farmers differently. Should Ruth excuse his penalty or apply the cooperative's rule without exception?
B: A scholarship requires every recipient to maintain eighty percent attendance. Administrator Joel sees that a refugee student fell just below the threshold while attending immigration appointments and will leave college without funding, yet other students lost awards under the same rule. Should Joel renew her scholarship as an exception or enforce the attendance standard equally?
C: A wholesaler wants three hundred peach crates packed by morning to catch the only train to market. Grower Helena can ship on time after quick visual sorting, or inspect every peach for bruising and miss the train, preserving quality but losing the week's buyers. Should Helena dispatch the crates quickly or delay them for careful inspection?

A: A laundromat charges the same replacement fee whenever customers lose a machine key. Owner Hamid meets an elderly customer who lost hers during an emergency evacuation and cannot afford both the fee and groceries, though everyone else has paid. Should Hamid replace her key without charge or follow the stated rule for every customer?
B: The housing office grants extensions only when repair applications arrive before a fixed cutoff. Clerk Sarah receives a late form from a tenant who was hospitalized and now faces a winter without heat, while several other late applicants were denied. Should Sarah accept his application because of the hardship or enforce the deadline consistently?
C: Bicycle shop owner Lian can stock an innovative folding bike from a new maker whose design might attract adventurous commuters but has little reliability history. A proven model sells steadily and includes dependable replacement parts, though it offers customers nothing new. Should Lian take a chance on the experimental bicycle or order the predictable established model?

A: Epidemiologist Marta has managed obsessive-compulsive disorder throughout her field study. Telling her research team could explain why certain travel arrangements matter and help colleagues discuss mental health honestly, but it would disclose a diagnosis she has concealed throughout her career. Should Marta share her condition with the team or keep her medical information private?
B: Actor Remy drew on his experience of bankruptcy to prepare for a new role. Describing that history during rehearsals could help the cast understand his choices and invite deeper collaboration, but his finances remain painfully personal and may become theater gossip. Should Remy tell the company about his bankruptcy or keep the source of his performance private?
C: A prestigious polar institute offers glaciologist Hana leadership of a five-year expedition program. The role would establish her internationally but require long absences from the laboratory friends who share meals, childcare, and daily life with her. Should Hana accept the position that advances her career or remain with the close research community she has built?

A: Team captain Zoe recently began treatment for an eating disorder. Explaining it to teammates could help them avoid harmful comments and understand why she sometimes trains separately, but the diagnosis is intimate and she fears it spreading through the league. Should Zoe speak openly with the team or keep her health information confidential?
B: Physician Elena is returning to work after caring for a partner with addiction. Sharing that experience at a staff meeting could help colleagues understand her interest in compassionate treatment and invite honest discussion, but it would expose her partner's private struggle as well as her own. Should Elena tell the department or keep the family experience private?
C: Boxer Marcus plans daily footwork drills for three months to correct a weakness before his next bout. Tonight his favorite restaurant is hosting a long tasting dinner, and the drills feel tedious after work, but skipping them weakens the consistency improvement requires. Should Marcus complete his training session or spend the evening enjoying the meal?

A: Nurse Adele has dyslexia and uses extra checks when recording medication. Telling her unit could help coworkers understand the process and build more candid safety practices, but she has never disclosed the diagnosis and worries it will redefine how they see her competence. Should Adele explain her dyslexia to colleagues or keep the information private?
B: Farmer Gideon is receiving counseling after panic attacks began during lambing season. Sharing this with neighboring farmers could explain why he now requests backup and encourage others to discuss similar problems, but his treatment feels deeply personal in their small community. Should Gideon speak openly about the panic attacks or keep his health history confidential?
C: A rehabilitation center requires patients who arrive intoxicated to miss that day's therapy group. Counselor Priya meets a homeless patient who relapsed after learning his sister died and may lose his housing placement without attendance, while others have been excluded under the rule. Should Priya admit him as an exception or enforce the same restriction?

A: Fire inspector Calvin uses hearing aids but has hidden his hearing loss from coworkers. Explaining it could help the team communicate clearly during noisy inspections and make colleagues more candid about accommodations, yet the diagnosis is personal and may alter how they trust his judgment. Should Calvin disclose his hearing loss to the department or keep it confidential?
B: While leading a neighborhood flood committee, Soraya privately undergoes fertility treatment that often changes her availability. Telling volunteers could clarify sudden schedule changes and invite more honest planning, but it would expose a painful matter she has shared only with her partner. Should Soraya explain the treatment to the committee or keep her personal circumstances private?
C: Paramedic Lewis promised to cover a remote festival shift after two colleagues took leave. He wakes with severe vomiting, and withdrawing may leave the event below required medical staffing, but working twelve hours far from a hospital could dangerously worsen his dehydration. Should Lewis report for the duty he accepted or stay home to protect his health?

A: Community kitchen coordinator Malik grew up relying on food banks, a history he has never told the volunteers. Sharing it could explain his strict respect for guests and encourage others to discuss poverty without shame, but it would reveal family hardship he still guards closely. Should Malik tell the group about his childhood or keep that history private?
B: Software manager Alice takes medication for bipolar disorder and recently needed time away when her prescription changed. Disclosing the condition could help her team understand the absence and create frank conversations about workload, but it exposes medical information that may follow her professionally. Should Alice speak openly with the developers or keep her diagnosis confidential?
C: Each evening, volunteer Hana spends thirty minutes entering tool loans for a neighborhood workshop so missing equipment can be traced. Tonight the task is dull and a warm bath awaits after a long day, but skipping it will create a backlog and weaken the habit. Should Hana update the records now or choose the immediate comfort of the bath?

A: A nonprofit needs its donation app ready before a televised fundraiser on Sunday. Programmer Joel can launch the core payment flow after a brief test, capturing that audience, or postpone release to examine accessibility, refunds, and unusual card failures carefully. Should Joel ship the usable app before the fundraiser or delay it until the full experience is reliable?
B: A stadium's running track must reopen for school championships next week. Contractor Laila can apply one quick surface coat and meet the date, or add two carefully cured layers that provide better grip and durability but force organizers to reschedule. Should Laila finish the track quickly for the championships or delay reopening for higher-quality work?
C: A video platform offers developer Marco a large bonus to add automatic high-resolution playback as the default. The feature would increase subscriptions and his payout, but it would consume more electricity and network capacity for millions of viewers who never requested it. Should Marco pursue the bonus by enabling the feature or keep efficient playback to reduce the shared resource cost?

A: A publisher wants illustrator Celia's children's book delivered tomorrow for an important catalog deadline. She can submit the complete rough drawings tonight, or spend four more days correcting inconsistent characters and painting richer backgrounds, causing the title to miss the catalog. Should Celia deliver the adequate illustrations quickly or delay them until the artwork meets her standards?
B: A restaurant offers grower Malik a premium price for two hundred herb boxes by Friday. He can pack quickly after checking only the top leaves, or inspect every bunch for pests and freshness, missing the delivery window but protecting consistent quality. Should Malik send the boxes on schedule or take longer to examine and repack them carefully?
C: Gallery owner Petra learns that her closest artist friend submitted a forged residency certificate to qualify for a regional exhibition. Revealing it preserves an honest selection and correct public record but may end her friend's career after years of mutual support. Should Petra tell the selection panel the certificate is false or protect her friend by remaining silent?

A: A college wants its new chemistry course online before enrollment closes tomorrow. Designer Renee can publish the lectures with basic captions and quizzes, or spend another week checking terminology, adding accessible diagrams, and testing every exercise, costing the course its first cohort. Should Renee release the workable course immediately or wait until the materials are carefully finished?
B: After a storm, the council wants a pedestrian bridge reopened before Monday's commute. Engineer Idris can approve a rapid standard repair, or keep it closed another ten days while crews replace hidden corroded fittings and document each joint thoroughly. Should Idris restore access quickly or delay reopening to ensure the repair's quality?
C: Headteacher Miriam proposes replacing the school's handwritten graduation ledger with searchable digital records and printed certificates. Former pupils return each year to sign the leather-bound volume, and staff consider that act a link to generations before them. Should Miriam introduce the digital system or preserve the traditional ledger and its annual signing ritual?

A: Heavy rain is approaching, and orchard owner Tomas has one day to harvest pears for a supermarket order. Fast picking gets the fruit under cover but causes bruising and mixes unripe pears into crates; careful selection produces better boxes while leaving part of the crop exposed. Should Tomas harvest everything quickly or risk rain to maintain quality?
B: A museum asks programmer Nia to deliver its ticketing website before a holiday weekend. She can activate the tested booking pages now, or postpone launch to improve screen-reader navigation and verify complex group refunds, losing several busy days. Should Nia release the basic site on time or finish the slower, more dependable version?
C: Farmer Grace saved this season's reserve to repair a leaking barn roof before winter. Her hired shepherd's daughter needs an insulin pump that the family cannot afford, and paying for it would provide direct help but leave Grace's livestock and income exposed to storms. Should Grace fund the child's pump or preserve the farm's emergency reserve?

A: A hotel requests sixty dining chairs from carpenter Omar before its opening next week. He can meet the date with a simple finish and standard joints, or spend ten additional days strengthening each frame and matching the stain precisely, forcing the hotel to rent furniture. Should Omar deliver acceptable chairs quickly or delay them for finer workmanship?
B: A laboratory needs preliminary soil results before officials decide where to drill emergency wells. Analyst Yuki can send automated readings this afternoon, or spend three days rerunning outliers and manually checking contamination controls, delaying the decision. Should Yuki provide the early usable results or wait until the analysis is thoroughly verified?
C: Bakery owner Felix discovers that his best friend and business partner substituted cheap margarine while advertising their pastries as all-butter. Correcting the labels and informing customers protects the truth but could destroy his friend's reputation and their partnership. Should Felix disclose the substitution or remain silent to protect the person who built the bakery with him?

A: A mining company offers geologist Lara a highly paid consulting role mapping untouched mountain deposits. The income would clear her mortgage, but successful surveys would enable roads and extraction across habitat used by many species and downstream villages. Should Lara accept the lucrative mapping contract or refuse it because of the broad environmental and community costs?
B: Procurement officer Dean can earn free personal travel by choosing an airline rewards card for all municipal bookings. Its fares are consistently higher, spreading extra costs across thousands of taxpayers, while the points would fund a holiday he otherwise cannot afford. Should Dean select the card for his private reward or use the cheaper option for the public budget?
C: Botanist Rina can explore an isolated valley where undocumented plants may yield an unexpected discovery, though access and results are uncertain. A greenhouse project offers confirmed specimens, controlled conditions, and a guaranteed publication schedule but little surprise. Should Rina pursue the unpredictable field expedition or choose the secure research project with reliable outcomes?

A: A ski resort offers racer Stefan free lodging and prize support if he promotes unrestricted helicopter skiing. The sponsorship would finance his season, while increased flights would burn fuel, disturb wildlife, and bring noise across valleys used by residents and other visitors. Should Stefan accept the valuable sponsorship or decline because of the wider impact?
B: Packaging supplier Rafi can double his margin by selling restaurants disposable foam containers that local rules still permit. The deal would stabilize his small company, but millions of boxes would enter landfills and litter waterways maintained by the wider community. Should Rafi take the profitable contract or keep selling costlier compostable packaging to limit collective harm?
C: Runner Elise prefers training for short trail races, although her parents and club mates insist she should enter a prestigious road marathon. They have already announced her expected participation and say withdrawing would disappoint everyone supporting her. Should Elise choose the smaller races she enjoys or run the marathon to preserve their approval?

A: A drug company offers physician Nina a generous speaking fee to recommend its branded inhaler at professional meetings. A cheaper generic works equally well, and widespread adoption of the brand would raise costs across patients and insurance pools. Should Nina accept the paid speaking role for personal income or decline to avoid imposing broader healthcare costs?
B: A manufacturer promises researcher Caleb a large patent share if he develops a single-use sensor for laboratories. The disposable model could make him wealthy, but thousands of labs would discard batteries and plastic housings after every test when a reusable design is possible. Should Caleb pursue the profitable disposable sensor or develop the lower-waste alternative?
C: Cardiologist Amara is offered leadership of a renowned urban research center, giving her a path to international recognition. Taking it means leaving the rural clinic where nurses, patients, and neighbors have become her daily circle over eight years. Should Amara accept the prestigious post or remain with the close healthcare community that depends on her presence?

A: A developer offers zoning officer Marcus discounted ownership in a new tower if he supports removing its energy-efficiency requirements. The apartment would secure his retirement, while higher power use and emissions would burden future residents and the city's electrical system for decades. Should Marcus support the exemption for private gain or reject it to protect the wider public interest?
B: A luxury brand offers muralist Ana a major fee to cover a public wall with vinyl advertising that will be discarded each month. The contract would pay her studio rent, but repeated installations create substantial plastic waste and replace freely accessible neighborhood art. Should Ana accept the lucrative campaign or refuse because of its broader cultural and environmental cost?
C: A parks department can open a forest section for unsupervised overnight camping, giving visitors freedom to choose routes and sites but leaving uncertain fire and rescue risks. A designated campground has patrols, marked exits, and controlled fire pits. Should director Pablo allow open-ended backcountry camping or restrict visitors to the protected campground?

A: Organizer Julie can rent the community festival grounds to a private car show for a personal commission. Hundreds of vehicles would idle during demonstrations, bringing noise and exhaust to surrounding homes and a nearby school, while the payment would clear her debts. Should Julie secure the profitable booking or refuse because neighbors would bear the disruption?
B: Hospital buyer Kofi is offered a personal bonus by a supplier if his clinic switches to individually packaged disposable gowns. The contract rewards him and simplifies storage, but it creates far more plastic waste and disposal costs shared by patients and the municipality. Should Kofi choose the bonus-paying supplier or retain reusable gowns to reduce the collective burden?
C: A community workshop suspends anyone who damages equipment through prohibited use. Coordinator Lena learns that a refugee member broke a saw while building emergency furniture for his family and cannot afford private tools, though previous violators served suspensions. Should Lena waive the penalty because of his hardship or enforce the same rule for every member?
